paragraphs.heading: Only the present matters
paragraphs.text: A Markov chain is a model of something that moves between states at random, where the chance of each next event depends only on the state reached in the event before. This is called the Markov property, sometimes described as memorylessness. Knowing the full history adds nothing: predictions made from the present state alone are just as good. Put another way, once the present state is known, the future and the past are independent.

paragraphs.heading: The parts of a chain
paragraphs.text: Each change of state is called a transition, and the chances attached to these changes are transition probabilities. A chain is described by three things: its set of possible states, called the state space; a transition matrix giving the probability of each transition; and a starting state or starting distribution. By convention every possible state and transition is included, so a next state always exists and the process never ends. Steps are usually pictured as moments in time, yet they could just as well be steps of distance or any other discrete measurement.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds of chain
paragraphs.text: If the chain moves at separate time steps, it is a discrete-time Markov chain, or DTMC; if it runs in continuous time, it is a continuous-time Markov chain, or CTMC. The term Markov chain is usually kept for the discrete-time kind, though some authors use the words differently. Many applications use a finite or countably infinite state space, and such state spaces are more straightforward to analyse statistically.

paragraphs.heading: What can be predicted
paragraphs.text: Since the system changes at random, it is generally impossible to say for certain which state the chain will be in at some future point. What can be predicted are the statistical properties of its future. In many applications, those properties are what matter.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are used
paragraphs.text: Markov chains are used in many ways to model real-world processes statistically. They are also the basis of Markov chain Monte Carlo, a family of simulation methods for sampling from complex probability distributions. Those methods are applied in fields such as physics, biology, chemistry, finance, economics, Bayesian statistics, information theory, and signal and speech processing.

paragraphs.heading: Markov's own work
paragraphs.text: The chains are named after the Russian mathematician Andrey Markov, who published his first paper on them in 1906. He was motivated by a disagreement with Pavel Nekrasov, who claimed that the weak law of large numbers needed independence. He proved that, given certain conditions, a chain's average outcomes converge to a fixed vector of values, which established such a law without assuming independence. He later used chains to study how vowels are distributed in Alexander Pushkin's Eugene Onegin.

paragraphs.heading: Before and after Markov
paragraphs.text: Some of the ideas came earlier: Markov processes in continuous time were known long before his work, in the form of the Poisson process. Henri Poincaré turned to chains on finite groups in 1912 to understand card shuffling. In a 1931 paper Andrey Kolmogorov developed much of the early theory of continuous-time Markov processes. Working independently while studying Brownian movement, Sydney Chapman had derived what is now called the Chapman–Kolmogorov equation in 1928.
